explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Luke says "everyone went to his own town to register." (Luke 2:3) No grand march to the capital, just everybody heading home to sign the paperwork. I think half the empire was packing a bag at the same time.

Rome is where Caesar Augustus sits, so I get why you went there. But the text says "everyone went to his own town to register." (Luke 2:3) Nobody had to cross the whole empire to the emperor's front door. That would be one LONG line, friend.
The temple is a big, holy place, so it's a fair guess. But this census wasn't a temple matter at all. Luke says "everyone went to his own town to register." (Luke 2:3) Home town, not Jerusalem.

Right on the money, baker. Luke says Joseph "was from the house and line of David." (Luke 2:4) That's why Bethlehem, the city of David, is where he has to go. His family roots are pointing him down the road.

Aaron, Moses' brother and Israel's first high priest, is a famous name, so I see the pull. But Luke says Joseph "was from the house and line of David." (Luke 2:4) Bethlehem is called the city of David in the same verse. Aaron isn't in this story.

Saul was Israel's first king, so you're in the right neighborhood with a king. But Luke names a different one. Joseph "was from the house and line of David." (Luke 2:4) David is the name on Bethlehem's sign.
Not quite, friend. Luke says "While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born." (Luke 2:6) "There" means Bethlehem. They never made it back to Nazareth first.
Yes, baker. The text says "While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born." (Luke 2:6) They were still in Bethlehem when it happened. The baby arrived away from home.
That's right. Luke says Mary "laid Him in a manger." (Luke 2:7) A manger is a feeding trough for animals. Not what you'd pick for a newborn, but that's what the text says.

A basket would sure be cozy, but Luke never mentions one. He says Mary "laid Him in a manger." (Luke 2:7) I once tried to nap in a cookie tin, so I know how hard it is to get comfortable in the wrong container.
The temple isn't in this scene, baker. Mary and Joseph are in Bethlehem, and Luke says she "laid Him in a manger." (Luke 2:7) A manger is a feeding trough, a long way from a temple.

explanations.answer: No room for them in the inn
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Luke gives. Mary laid Him in a manger "because there was no room for them in the inn." (Luke 2:7) The text says nothing more about why, so I won't guess. It just says the inn had no room.

Luke never says anything about the price, friend. He says Mary laid Him in a manger "because there was no room for them in the inn." (Luke 2:7) No room, plain and simple. I'm not adding a price tag the text doesn't have.
That's a story Luke doesn't tell. The text gives one reason: "there was no room for them in the inn." (Luke 2:7) Nobody gets sent away in this verse. Let's keep to what's written, baker.

You got it, baker. Luke says "an angel of the Lord stood before them." (Luke 2:9) Right there in the field, in the middle of the night shift. Those shepherds clocked in for an ordinary night and got a visitor from heaven.

Elijah, the prophet who spoke for God long before this, does show up later in Luke, but not here. In this scene "an angel of the Lord stood before them." (Luke 2:9) No prophet is mentioned in this field.
With Caesar's census going on, a soldier isn't a crazy guess. But Luke says "an angel of the Lord stood before them." (Luke 2:9) No soldiers in this scene, just shepherds and a visitor from heaven.
Yes, baker. Luke says "they were terrified." (Luke 2:9) An angel appears and the glory of the Lord shines around them. I think I'd have dropped my whole tray of cookies.
Joy is coming, friend, but not yet. Luke says of the shepherds, "they were terrified." (Luke 2:9) The good news of great joy comes in the next verse, after the angel speaks.
Curious is a pretty calm word for this moment. The text says "they were terrified." (Luke 2:9) An angel stood before them and the glory of the Lord shone around them. That's a lot more than curious.
Close, but no. The angel says the good news "will be for all the people." (Luke 2:10) The shepherds are the first to hear it, but they're not the only ones it's for.
Right, baker. The angel says it is "good news of great joy that will be for all the people." (Luke 2:10) The shepherds hear it first, but it's meant for everybody. That's a big circle.
That's the one. The angel says, "He is Christ the Lord!" (Luke 2:11) He also says this baby is a Savior born in the city of David. That's a LOT of title for someone lying in a manger.

explanations.answer: A prophet of the Most High
explanations.explanation: A prophet speaks for God, so I see why you picked it. But the angel says something bigger: "He is Christ the Lord!" (Luke 2:11) That's the title he gives this baby.
Zechariah was the priest in Luke 1, so the name is fresh in your mind. But the angel doesn't call this baby a priest. He says, "He is Christ the Lord!" (Luke 2:11)

explanations.answer: Let's go to Bethlehem and see
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. They say, "Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us." (Luke 2:15) No long meeting, no committee. They heard it, and they wanted to go see it.
Waiting for daylight sounds sensible, friend. But the shepherds say, "Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened…" (Luke 2:15) Nothing in the text has them waiting for morning.

explanations.answer: Let's ask the town elders first
explanations.explanation: The elders never come up in this story, baker. The shepherds say, "Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us." (Luke 2:15) They go straight to the source, no permission slip needed.
Not this time, friend. Luke says "they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby." (Luke 2:16) Hurried is the opposite of taking their time.
Yes, baker. The text says "they hurried off." (Luke 2:16) No stopping for a snack, no slow stroll. I think I'd have been running with my apron flapping.
That's not what happened, baker. Luke says, "After they had seen the Child, they spread the message they had received about Him." (Luke 2:17) They told people instead of keeping it quiet.

Right on, friend. They "spread the message they had received about Him." (Luke 2:17) These shepherds saw the Child and went telling everybody. I think it would've been hard to keep quiet after a night like that.

That's right. Luke says "all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them." (Luke 2:18) Shepherds show up with a message about a baby in a manger. I'd have stopped what I was doing to listen too.
Nobody gets angry in this verse, baker. Luke says "all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them." (Luke 2:18) Amazed is the word the text uses.
Doubt is a fair human reaction, but it's not the one Luke gives. He says "all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them." (Luke 2:18) Amazed is the word.

explanations.answer: Treasures them up and ponders them
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Luke says "Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart." (Luke 2:19) While others were amazed out loud, she kept these things close and thought them over.
That's what the shepherds do, not Mary. Luke says "Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart." (Luke 2:19) The text doesn't have her telling the town.
Luke doesn't have Mary asking Joseph anything here. He says "Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart." (Luke 2:19) She holds on to it and thinks it over.

You got it, baker. Luke says "The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen." (Luke 2:20) They went back to the same fields, but I bet it felt like a whole new place.
No arguing in this story, friend. The shepherds returned "glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen." (Luke 2:20) They were on the same page, and it was a good page.
Luke never says a word about worry over the flocks, baker. He says the shepherds returned "glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen." (Luke 2:20) Praise is what he gives us.

That's right, baker. Luke says all they heard and saw was "just as the angel had told them." (Luke 2:20) The angel gave them a sign, and they found the Baby lying in the manger (Luke 2:12, 16). It all matched up.

Not quite, friend. Luke says what they heard and saw "was just as the angel had told them." (Luke 2:20) The angel said they'd find a baby in a manger (Luke 2:12), and that's what they found. No surprises, no mismatches.
